41903.etyen:
From okse (“ox”) + tunge (“tongue”), literally “ox tongue”. In the botanical sense, the name refers to the shape and roughness of the leaves; compare Latin buglossa (“ox tongue”), from Ancient Greek βούγλωσσον (boúglōsson, “ox tongue”).
Parallel formations include Norwegian Nynorsk oksetunge, Danish oksetunge, Swedish oxtunga, German Ochsenzunge, Dutch ossentong, and English oxtongue.

1000623.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Dutch Nederland (“the Netherlands; literally “low land””), formed from neder (“down, low”) and land (“land, country”). The name refers to the country's low-lying geography.
The first element derives from Middle Dutch nēder (“down, lower”), from Old Dutch *nithar (“down”), from Proto-West Germanic *niþer (“down, below”), from Proto-Germanic *niþer (“down, below”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *niter (“down”). The second derives from Middle Dutch lant (“land”), from Old Dutch lant (“land”), from Proto-West Germanic *land (“land”), from Proto-Germanic *landą (“la

1001135.etyen:
Either a feminine derivative of Emil (“male given name”), or ultimately from Latin Aemilia (“female given name”), the feminine form of the Roman nomen Aemilius. The Latin name is traditionally connected with aemulus (“eager; emulating, rivaling”).
Compare Danish Emilia, Swedish Emilia, Finnish Emilia, Italian Emilia and English Emily.

en.g: a male given name from Old Norse

1001391.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Kári (“male given name”), originally a byname meaning “curly-haired”, related to kárr (“curly-haired; curly, curved”). Thus, the name originally meant “the curly-haired one”. The Norwegian form reflects the development of Old Norse á to å and final -i to -e.
Compare Danish Kåre, Swedish Kåre, Icelandic Kári and Faroese Kári (“male given name”).

1004207.etyen: abbor + ruse, first part from Old Danish aghborre (“perch”) and Old Swedish aghborre, aborre (“perch”), the beginning of the word comes from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”) + the end of the word comes from Old Norse borrablað, from Proto-Germanic *burzô. Last part possibly from a Celtic word, from Gaulish rusca, from Proto-Celtic *rūskos (“bark”), possibly from earlier *rukskos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewk- (“to dig, till (soil)”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to move, stir, rise, quarrel”) or *Hrew- (“to tear out, dig out, open, acquire”).

i Oslo … gikk en hel by i rosetog for terrormarerittets ofre og etterlatte
In Oslo … an entire city took part in a rose march for the victims and bereaved of the terror nightmare.

1004975.etyen: rose (“rose”) + tog (“procession, parade”), literally “rose procession”. The word became especially prominent following the terrorist attacks of 22 July 2011, when large memorial gatherings involving roses were held throughout Norway. It was selected by Språkrådet (“Language Council of Norway”) as its Word of the Year for 2011.
